ideas.author: John W. Campbell

ideas.author: James Schmitz

ideas.author: James Tiptree, Jr.

ideas.line: A complete atomic power source small enough to hold between two fingers.
ideas.name: Tiny Nuclear Generator
ideas.profit: a monopoly-like profit, kept by licence holders

verdict.money_why: Firms working far from a grid buy it, and because governments let only a few hands hold nuclear fuel, the few permitted makers keep what is left.
verdict.prize_why: A complete atomic power source held between two fingers would change what it costs to power machines anywhere.

ideas.author: Isaac Asimov
ideas.line: Workshop cutting tools driven by a small atomic power source.
ideas.name: Nuclear Shears
ideas.profit: a fat profit, kept by licence holders

verdict.money_why: Workshops buy them, and many toolmakers could build them once the power source exists, so no seller keeps much.
verdict.prize_why: Powerful workshop cutters are a better tool for a trade, not a new industry.

ideas.author: Jack Vance
ideas.line: Trees bred to grow large hollow pods that people move into and live in as homes.
ideas.name: House Trees
ideas.profit: competed away to users

verdict.money_why: People buy it as a home, and since living stock multiplies once any of it is sold, no originator can hold it, so the growers, builders and landowners that already hold stock, sites and the trade of housing collect.
verdict.prize_why: Homes that grow by themselves would sharply cut the cost of housing.

ideas.author: Neal Stephenson
ideas.line: A dust-sized machine built for one specific job.
ideas.name: Mite
ideas.profit: a moderate profit, kept by the maker

verdict.money_why: Firms buy them for their work, assuming many jobs are served, and once one maker shows how, established equipment makers copy and collect.
verdict.prize_why: Dust-sized machines each built for a job would be a new kind of tool for cleaning, repair, sensing and medicine.

ideas.author: William Gibson
ideas.line: Huge towers grown from molecularly engineered fibres.
ideas.name: Nanotech Buildings
ideas.profit: no lasting profit

verdict.money_why: Developers buy them, as with towers today, and once the method is known the big builders with land and crews collect.
verdict.prize_why: Growing huge towers from engineered fibre would change the cost of building, which is more than simply building taller.

ideas.author: Sid Meier
ideas.line: An adaptive biological lubricant that improves itself with use.
ideas.name: Organic Superlubricant
ideas.profit: competed away to users

verdict.money_why: Machine owners buy it, and a living lubricant can be grown by many suppliers, so no seller keeps much.
verdict.prize_why: A lubricant that improves with use is a better supply for machines, not a new industry.

ideas.author: Harl Vincent
ideas.line: A pistol that fires a beam of energy instead of bullets.
ideas.name: Ray-Pistol
ideas.profit: a fat profit, kept by incumbent firms

verdict.money_why: Armies buy it with public money, and since rival makers can copy it the established arms suppliers with standing army contracts collect.
verdict.prize_why: A beam weapon carried in the hand does much the same job as a gun, so the gain over a gun is modest.

verdict.prize_why: Carried in the hand, it does much the same job as a gun, so the gain over a gun is modest.

ideas.author: Yoshiyuki Tomino
ideas.line: A giant orbital mirror weapon used in a space war in the series.
ideas.name: Solar Flare System
ideas.profit: not judged (not a technology, not something sold, not physically possible, or unclear)

verdict.money_why: Only governments pay, and the few shipyards and space builders that already hold such contracts are the ones able to deliver it, so they collect.
verdict.prize_why: A heavy beam or a weapon fired from orbit lets a state strike or defend across great distances and would take a large share of what it spends on arms.

ideas.author: David Drake
ideas.line: A hovering armoured war vehicle that runs on its own onboard fusion reactor.
ideas.name: Supertank
ideas.profit: a fat profit, kept by the maker

verdict.money_why: Armies pay, and since the designs can be copied, the builders that already own the works and hold the army's supply contracts collect.
verdict.prize_why: Armoured fighting vehicles and warcraft are among the biggest things an army buys, and a better one shifts what winning costs.

ideas.author: Neal Stephenson
ideas.line: A fictional cyborg guard animal that protects property in the story.
ideas.name: Rat Thing
ideas.profit: no lasting profit

verdict.money_why: Property owners and security firms pay, and since others could learn to join animal and machine once one firm had done it, the security suppliers that already serve those buyers collect.
verdict.prize_why: A guard animal rebuilt as a machine protects property better than a dog but serves a niche of security buyers.

ideas.author: John Varley
ideas.line: Engineered weather staged as an artistic performance.
ideas.name: Environmental Happening
ideas.profit: not judged (not a technology, not something sold, not physically possible, or unclear)

verdict.money_why: I assumed spectators and patrons pay the performers, and anyone with the gear and the skill can stage one, so no seller keeps much.
verdict.prize_why: Weather shaped as a show is an entertainment for a small audience.

ideas.author: Roger Zelazny
ideas.line: A project to make new land by deliberately triggering volcanoes under the sea.
ideas.name: RUMOKO
ideas.profit: not judged (not a technology, not something sold, not physically possible, or unclear)

verdict.money_why: A government pays for a project of this size, and I assumed the heavy engineering firms that already win such contracts do the work and collect.
verdict.prize_why: New land raised from the sea would be worth a great deal to a crowded country.

ideas.author: Thomas A. Easton

ideas.profit: a fat profit, kept by incumbent firms

verdict.prize_why: A house that grows itself would cut the cost of building homes, assuming it grows cheaply.

ideas.author: Greg Bear
ideas.line: A living floor covering that consumes the dirt and debris that falls onto it.

verdict.prize_why: A carpet that eats its own dirt saves some cleaning of floors.

ideas.author: Edmond Hamilton
ideas.line: Travel papers that people need to journey between worlds.

ideas.profit: not judged (not a technology, not something sold, not physically possible, or unclear)

verdict.money_why: Nothing is sold, so nobody pays and no seller keeps anything.
verdict.prize_why: Permits, papers and traffic rules for space travel are set by governments, not sold as a product.

ideas.author: Philip K. Dick
